transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I came because I keep hearing people talking about me—like through the conference room walls, or sometimes from my phone even when it’s off. It’s usually board members or staff saying I’m ruining the company, and it sounds so clear I answer them before I realize… no one else heard it. Which is embarrassing, because I’m usually very composed in meetings, I mean, I’ve handled tense rooms before, quarterly reviews, investor calls, all of that, but this is different. It feels like they’re right there.
Have you been feeling unusually high, energized, or irritable lately?

I don’t know that I’d call it “high.” Energized… I mean, I’m always running at a pretty high level, or I was supposed to be—when you’re the one everyone looks to, you can’t exactly come in flat, right? But unusually? I’m not sure.

I do get irritated when people ask me the same thing twice in meetings, especially if they should already know the numbers, but that’s always been… I mean, that’s leadership. Or it was. I guess I’m not sure what you mean by unusually.
Do you believe people at work are actually trying to harm your position or reputation?

I… I don’t know. “Harm” sounds so dramatic, like legal language, and I’ve sat through enough compliance briefings to know people use that word when they want minutes taken and counsel in the room.

At work, people talk. They always talk. Sometimes it feels pointed, like there are conversations happening just outside where I can pin them down, but whether they’re actually trying to damage my position or reputation… I’m not sure. I keep trying to sort it out like a business problem, you know, motives, incentives, who benefits, but then I end up thinking about old board dynamics and the last restructuring and it gets all tangled.

So… I can’t say for certain. I don’t have proof, if that’s what you mean.
Have you needed much less sleep than usual lately and still felt rested?

Sleep is… hard to measure, honestly. I mean, I used to track everything—calendar blocks, calls across time zones, even how long I’d sit in traffic—so you’d think I could give you a clean number. But lately it’s not clean like that.

I don’t know if I’ve needed much less sleep and felt rested. Some mornings I get up because there are things to handle, or because I’m already thinking through what has to happen next, but “rested” isn’t really the word I’d use. I’m not sure.
Have you been feeling depressed most of the day?

Depressed most of the day… I don’t know. That’s a big word, isn’t it? I mean, people say “depressed” when a quarterly report is bad, too, which always bothered me because it makes everything sound like a market condition.

I’ve had low moments, I guess, or times where things feel… heavy. But most of the day? I’m not sure I could divide the day up that neatly. Some of it I’m just trying to get through what’s in front of me, and then my mind goes somewhere else, and by the time I notice what I’m feeling, the whole morning’s gone.

So I don’t know if I’d say depressed most of the day. I’m not sure.
Have other people told you that your speech or thoughts are hard to follow or seem disorganized?

I don’t… I don’t think people have said it that directly. “Hard to follow” is sort of a subjective thing, isn’t it? In meetings, people used to say I was “big picture,” which can mean anything depending on whether they liked the direction or not.

Sometimes someone asks me to go back or clarify what I meant, but that happens in strategy discussions all the time. You start with revenue, then you have to talk about staffing, then legal, then someone brings up a vendor contract from three years ago and suddenly everyone acts like you changed the subject when really it’s all connected.

So… I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed people telling me my thoughts are disorganized, not in those words.
Have you recently felt more powerful, important, or capable than usual?

More powerful? I don’t… I’m not sure I’d put it that way.

I mean, in my old role, you had to sound certain even when things were moving underneath you. If you walked into a room and said, “I feel sort of capable today,” nobody would follow you anywhere. So confidence becomes part of the furniture, you know? Like the glass conference table we had that everyone hated because it showed fingerprints, but the board chair insisted it made the room look “transparent.”

Lately, I don’t know if I feel more important than usual. I have thoughts about what needs to be handled, but that’s not the same as feeling powerful. I haven’t really measured it that way.
Have you used any drugs recently, including cannabis, cocaine, amphetamines, hallucinogens, or non-prescribed pills?

Drugs recently… I don’t think so. I mean, “used” is a funny word because people use all kinds of things to get through a day—coffee, cold medicine, those little peppermint things they put in hotel lobbies that taste like chalk.

But cannabis or cocaine or… no, I don’t think so. Non-prescribed pills—I’d have to think what counts. I’m not someone who, you know, has a drawer full of mystery tablets or anything. I haven’t been doing that.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, “interest” is such a slippery word because sometimes you still know something matters, like work matters, the agenda matters, the people waiting for a decision matter, but it’s like the cord isn’t plugged in.

I used to be the one pushing every idea forward, calling people after openings, following up on details no one else even noticed. I liked that, or I think I did. It had energy. Now I can sit at my desk for hours just looking at the agenda, and it’s just… paper. Or a screen. I don’t feel much about it.

And at home, too, I barely talk to my husband sometimes. At work I don’t say much to staff unless I absolutely have to. It’s strange because there are all these things I used to care about, and now I mostly just feel kind of blank.
Have the voices ever happened during a time when you were not feeling down or blank?

Yes… I think so. It isn’t only when I feel blank. That’s the thing that makes it hard to explain, because people want it to fit into a neat box, like quarterly reporting, where the numbers either go up or down and everyone pretends that means they understand the company.

I’ve heard them at work, through the conference room walls, like board members or staff talking about me—saying I’m ruining everything, ruining the company. And sometimes it comes from my phone, even when it’s off, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud, but it’s clear. Clear enough that I answer before I realize no one else heard anything. Then everyone looks at me like I’ve interrupted a meeting that wasn’t happening.
Did the voices start after a physical illness, head injury, or seizure?

I don’t know. I mean, I don’t remember some big thing like that—like falling and hitting my head and then suddenly everything changed. Seizure… I don’t think I’ve had one, unless there are kinds people don’t notice, which is a strange thought.

Physical illness… I’ve been sick like normal people get sick, colds and things, but I don’t have a neat before-and-after for it. It’s not like the annual report where you can point to the quarter it started and say, there, that’s where the line drops. So… I’m not sure. I haven’t noticed it starting after anything like that.
Have you been hearing these voices for longer than one month?

Yes… longer than a month. I think it’s been about three months now, the voices through the walls or from my phone.

It’s hard to mark exactly because time gets mixed up, you know, with meetings and deadlines and all those little calendar reminders, but… yes. Not just a few days. More like three months.
Have you felt that someone or something is controlling your thoughts or putting thoughts into your mind?

I… don’t know. “Controlling” is a big word. I wouldn’t say it like someone has a remote control, you know, like changing the channel in my head.

Sometimes thoughts feel crowded, like too many people walked into the room at once and nobody checked the meeting agenda, but that’s not the same thing as someone putting them there, I guess. I haven’t really noticed it that way. Or… I’m not sure what would count.
Do you believe anyone is deliberately plotting against you?

Plotting… I don’t know. That sounds very organized, like a committee with minutes and action items, and people aren’t usually that competent, honestly.

I mean, in business, people say they’re “aligned,” and then three departments are quietly doing completely different things, so when you ask if someone is deliberately plotting, I… I’m not sure I’d call it that. I haven’t seen, like, a plan or proof.

Sometimes I wonder about people’s motives, but that’s also just life, isn’t it? People have agendas. But against me specifically… I don’t know. I can’t really say yes to that.
Do you feel that you have done something terribly wrong or caused serious harm?

Terribly wrong… I mean, I’ve made mistakes. Everybody makes mistakes. In an executive role, you sign off on things and then six months later someone says the projections were optimistic, but that’s not the same as harm, exactly.

I don’t know if you mean like morally wrong, or legally wrong, or just… feeling responsible for things. Sometimes I replay conversations and think I should’ve said something differently, but caused serious harm? I don’t have a clear thing like that. I’m not sure.
For at least two weeks, have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless nearly every day?

I don’t know if I’d call it “depressed.” That word feels… heavy, like it belongs on a form somewhere with boxes you tick.

I’ve had days where things feel flat, or I don’t really want to deal with people, but then work has its own weather system, you know? One bad meeting can make the whole week look gray, and then suddenly someone sends a nonsense email at 10 p.m. and I’m irritated instead of sad, which is different.

Nearly every day for two weeks… I’m not sure I’ve been tracking it like that. I can’t really say yes.
Have you found yourself talking much less than you used to?

Yes… I think so. I used to be the one talking all the time, honestly. In meetings, I’d be the person pushing ideas forward, calling people after openings, following up on every little thing because if you don’t, it all turns into fog.

Now I can sit at my desk with the agenda right in front of me, and I just… stare at it. Hours can go by. It’s embarrassing, because people expect me to have something to say. My staff will come in and I’ll give these short answers, or nothing much at all.

Even at home, with my husband, I barely talk sometimes. And it’s not like I’m trying to punish anyone or make a point. It’s just… there’s nothing there. Work used to light me up, and now I can barely get words out about it.
Have these experiences made it hard for you to do your job or manage daily life the way you used to?

Yes. I mean… I hate saying it that plainly, but yes.

At work, I’m not really running the division the way I used to. People still look at me like I’m supposed to decide, and I’ll have the file open, the numbers there, and I just don’t make the call. Then later I find out one of the senior people has “handled it,” which is their polite way of saying they couldn’t wait for me anymore.

It’s strange, because I used to be very good at that—keeping the whole machine moving. Now basic executive decisions feel like trying to lift furniture underwater. And at home it’s not much better. My husband has been doing most of the household things because I either start something and leave it half done, or I don’t start it at all.

Like the mail piles up, or something needs scheduling, and I think, yes, in a minute… and then the whole day is gone. So yes, it’s made things hard. More than I want people to know.
Was there a time when you felt sad or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

I don’t really know how to separate “sad” from… I don’t know, being worn down, or being quiet, or just not having the motor running.

Most of the day, nearly every day—that sounds very exact. I didn’t mark it on a calendar or anything. There were stretches where everything felt heavy, but then something at work would happen and I’d be annoyed, or I’d be focused on some stupid email thread about budgets, and then I think, well, is that sadness? Or is that just Tuesday?

So I can’t honestly say yes to that the way you’re asking it. I’m not sure.
At any point during the last few months, did you feel sad or hopeless nearly all day, almost every day?

I… I don’t know. “Nearly all day, almost every day” is hard for me to say yes to, because I don’t track it like that.

There were days where I felt low, I guess, or like the room had gotten smaller, but then I’d get pulled into some work thing, or I’d be thinking about whether the cleaners came on Thursday or Friday—actually that changed because of the building schedule—and then I don’t know if that counts as hopeless.

So… I’m not sure. I can’t really give you a clean yes or no.

patient.answer:
I… don’t know. “Controlling” is a big word. I wouldn’t say it like someone has a remote control, you know, like changing the channel in my head.

Sometimes thoughts feel crowded, like too many people walked into the room at once and nobody checked the meeting agenda, but that’s not the same thing as someone putting them there, I guess. I haven’t really noticed it that way. Or… I’m not sure what would count.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there are prominent delusional beliefs beyond auditory hallucinations, to distinguish delusional disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis and psychotic depression.
doctor.question: Do you believe anyone is deliberately plotting against you?

target_item.reason: The question is about persecutory delusions or paranoia—believing someone is deliberately plotting against me—which is not covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Plotting… I don’t know. That sounds very organized, like a committee with minutes and action items, and people aren’t usually that competent, honestly.

I mean, in business, people say they’re “aligned,” and then three departments are quietly doing completely different things, so when you ask if someone is deliberately plotting, I… I’m not sure I’d call it that. I haven’t seen, like, a plan or proof.

Sometimes I wonder about people’s motives, but that’s also just life, isn’t it? People have agendas. But against me specifically… I don’t know. I can’t really say yes to that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent mood-congruent guilt/worthlessness delusions suggesting major depressive disorder with psychotic features rather than a primary psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Do you feel that you have done something terribly wrong or caused serious harm?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about excessive guilt or belief that one has caused serious harm, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Terribly wrong… I mean, I’ve made mistakes. Everybody makes mistakes. In an executive role, you sign off on things and then six months later someone says the projections were optimistic, but that’s not the same as harm, exactly.

I don’t know if you mean like morally wrong, or legally wrong, or just… feeling responsible for things. Sometimes I replay conversations and think I should’ve said something differently, but caused serious harm? I don’t have a clear thing like that. I’m not sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a sustained period of depressed mood long enough to support a major depressive episode, helping distinguish schizoaffective disorder or psychotic depression from schizophrenia or delusional disorder.
doctor.question: For at least two weeks, have you felt down, depressed, or hopeless nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The question is about depressed mood or hopelessness for at least two weeks, which is not covered by the provided schizophrenia symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d call it “depressed.” That word feels… heavy, like it belongs on a form somewhere with boxes you tick.

I’ve had days where things feel flat, or I don’t really want to deal with people, but then work has its own weather system, you know? One bad meeting can make the whole week look gray, and then suddenly someone sends a nonsense email at 10 p.m. and I’m irritated instead of sad, which is different.

Nearly every day for two weeks… I’m not sure I’ve been tracking it like that. I can’t really say yes.

doctor.intent: Assess whether prominent negative symptoms are present, which would support schizophrenia over delusional disorder, major depressive disorder with psychotic features, schizoaffective disorder, or psychotic disorder due to a medical condition.
doctor.question: Have you found yourself talking much less than you used to?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I used to be the person driving every idea and calling people after openings, but now I can sit at my desk for hours staring at the agenda, barely speak to my husband or staff, and feel almost nothing about work I used to love.
target_item.reason: The question asks about reduced speech compared with before, which is directly covered by diminished speech under negative symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. I used to be the one talking all the time, honestly. In meetings, I’d be the person pushing ideas forward, calling people after openings, following up on every little thing because if you don’t, it all turns into fog.

Now I can sit at my desk with the agenda right in front of me, and I just… stare at it. Hours can go by. It’s embarrassing, because people expect me to have something to say. My staff will come in and I’ll give these short answers, or nothing much at all.

Even at home, with my husband, I barely talk sometimes. And it’s not like I’m trying to punish anyone or make a point. It’s just… there’s nothing there. Work used to light me up, and now I can barely get words out about it.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether there has been a sustained psychotic syndrome with prominent deterioration in functioning outside of mood episodes, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder, major depressive disorder with psychotic features, and delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Have these experiences made it hard for you to do your job or manage daily life the way you used to?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m no longer reliably able to run the division or keep up with basic executive decisions, and senior staff have quietly taken over work I used to handle myself. At home, my husband has had to manage most household responsibilities because I leave things unfinished or do not start them at all.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the experiences have affected the patient’s ability to work and manage daily life, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean… I hate saying it that plainly, but yes.

At work, I’m not really running the division the way I used to. People still look at me like I’m supposed to decide, and I’ll have the file open, the numbers there, and I just don’t make the call. Then later I find out one of the senior people has “handled it,” which is their polite way of saying they couldn’t wait for me anymore.

It’s strange, because I used to be very good at that—keeping the whole machine moving. Now basic executive decisions feel like trying to lift furniture underwater. And at home it’s not much better. My husband has been doing most of the household things because I either start something and leave it half done, or I don’t start it at all.

Like the mail piles up, or something needs scheduling, and I think, yes, in a minute… and then the whole day is gone. So yes, it’s made things hard. More than I want people to know.

inference.note: Dropped F22 because persistent auditory hallucinations with marked functional decline and negative symptoms are not typical for delusional disorder. Dropped F06.0 because there is no supporting history of a medical/neurologic trigger, while symptoms have persisted about 3 months. Remaining differential is led by schizophrenia, with schizoaffective depressive type and severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms still possible but less supported because hallucinations also occur outside clear depressive episodes.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a distinct period of depressed mood occurring most of the time for at least two weeks, to separate schizoaffective depressive type or major depressive disorder with psychotic features from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Was there a time when you felt sad or hopeless most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about depressed mood or hopelessness for a possible depressive episode, which is not covered by the provided schizophrenia symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know how to separate “sad” from… I don’t know, being worn down, or being quiet, or just not having the motor running.

Most of the day, nearly every day—that sounds very exact. I didn’t mark it on a calendar or anything. There were stretches where everything felt heavy, but then something at work would happen and I’d be annoyed, or I’d be focused on some stupid email thread about budgets, and then I think, well, is that sadness? Or is that just Tuesday?

So I can’t honestly say yes to that the way you’re asking it. I’m not sure.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has ever been a clear major depressive episode, to distinguish schizoaffective disorder or psychotic depression from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: At any point during the last few months, did you feel sad or hopeless nearly all day, almost every day?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about sustained sad or hopeless mood over the last few months, which is not covered by the listed schizophrenia symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t know. “Nearly all day, almost every day” is hard for me to say yes to, because I don’t track it like that.

There were days where I felt low, I guess, or like the room had gotten smaller, but then I’d get pulled into some work thing, or I’d be thinking about whether the cleaners came on Thursday or Friday—actually that changed because of the building schedule—and then I don’t know if that counts as hopeless.

So… I’m not sure. I can’t really give you a clean yes or no.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking help today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports persistent auditory hallucinations for about 3 months, occurring even outside periods of feeling 'blank' or low, with no clear evidence of a full depressive episode and no evidence of mania. Psychotic symptoms are therefore primary rather than mood-congruent or mood-dependent. Functional decline at work and home is clearly present. This most strongly supports schizophrenia, paranoid subtype, over schizoaffective disorder depressive type or severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms.
